extra.message: The 404 error handler builds a Jinja2 template string by f-string-interpolating request.path (fully attacker-controlled URL path) and then passes it to render_template_string(), which compiles and executes it as a Jinja2 template. A request to a path such as '/{{7*7}}' or a path containing '{{ config }} ' / '{{ self.__init__.__globals__.__builtins__.__import__("os").popen("id").read() }}' will be evaluated server-side, leading to Server-Side Template Injection and full remote code execution.

extra.message: The 'search' query parameter (request.args.get('search', ''), line 27) is concatenated directly into a raw SQL fragment via an f-string and passed to sqlalchemy.text(), then used as a filter in the ORM query. A value like "' UNION SELECT ... --" breaks out of the LIKE clause, allowing SQL injection (e.g. to read other users' private notes or exfiltrate data via UNION-based injection).

In validate_token(), the user-supplied 'registration_code' form field (code) is interpolated directly into a raw SQL query string via an f-string and executed with session.execute(text(...)). An attacker can inject SQL, e.g. registration_code="' UNION SELECT id, code FROM users --" style payloads adapted to this table, to bypass registration-code validation or extract data via UNION-based injection.

update_account() takes every field submitted in AccountForm (email, password, password_control, is_admin) except 'password', and blindly mass-assigns it onto current_user via __dict__.update() followed by session.merge(). Because AccountForm defines an 'is_admin' BooleanField, any authenticated user can POST is_admin=true to /account and grant themselves admin privileges. This is a critical privilege-escalation / mass-assignment vulnerability.

extra.message: before_request() reads the client-supplied 'preferences' cookie and passes it through base64-decode into pickle.loads(). Flask's set_cookie here is not cryptographically signed (raw b64encode(pickle.dumps(...)) is used, not the signed session cookie), so an attacker can craft an arbitrary pickle payload (e.g. via a class with __reduce__ invoking os.system) and set it as the 'preferences' cookie to achieve remote code execution on every subsequent request.

download() calls urllib.request.urlopen(url) with a URL taken directly from user input (ImageForm.url in routes/account.py add_image, line 60-61), with no scheme or host allow-listing. urlopen supports the 'file://' scheme by default, so a value like 'file:///etc/passwd' reads arbitrary local files (which are then base64-encoded and stored/displayed as the user's profile image), and http(s) URLs allow requests to internal/cloud-metadata hosts (e.g. http://169.254.169.254/...), enabling SSRF.

extra.message: delete_note(note_id) only checks @login_required and that the note exists; it never verifies that note.user_id == current_user.id (or that current_user is an admin) before deleting. Any authenticated user can delete any other user's notes by guessing/incrementing note_id, resulting in broken access control / IDOR on a destructive action.

extra.message: note.text (free-form user input from NoteForm's TextAreaField, routes/notes.py add_note) is rendered with the Jinja2 '| safe' filter, disabling autoescaping. Since notes are shared with other users when not private (utils/notes.py returns all non-private notes plus the owner's own notes), any user can store a note containing '<script>...</script>' or other HTML/JS which will execute in the browser of every other user who views the home page — persistent/stored XSS.

extra.message: The application uses plain WTForms Form classes (not FlaskForm / Flask-WTF) with no CSRF token generation or validation anywhere in the codebase (no csrf_token() usage in any template, no CSRFProtect configured). All state-changing POST endpoints (/account, /notes, /notes/<id>/delete, /registration-codes, /account/image) are vulnerable to Cross-Site Request Forgery. This is especially severe combined with the mass-assignment privilege-escalation issue on /account: a forged cross-site POST can silently grant is_admin=true to a logged-in victim.

app.secret_key is hardcoded to the static string 'super secret key'. This key signs Flask's session cookie; an attacker who knows/guesses it (it is also publicly visible in this repository) can forge arbitrary session cookies, including impersonating any user_id via flask_login's session, resulting in authentication bypass.
